say.text: Hour 3. A 70 kg adult with a 40% burn is on the formula rate of 700 mL/h.
Urine has run at 15 mL/h for the last hour. What do you do?

choices.label: Carry on at 700 mL/h, exactly as calculated
Raise the rate about 20–25% and recheck urine hourly
Cut the rate by 20–25% to protect the kidneys
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what the urine is telling you about how well the tissues are being filled.
That is not the right choice.
Keeping the formula rate feels safe, since the number is already worked out. But the formula is only a starting estimate, and the hourly urine is the feedback that changes it.

sure_note.text: You were sure, and this is the commonest management error. Treat the formula as a start and let the urine speak every hour.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Cutting feels like protecting the kidneys from overload. But low output points to under-filling, and cutting the rate starves the tissues further.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look at what low urine output signals about the tissues.

say.text: The formula sets a starting rate, not a final one. The urine shows whether the tissues are filled.
The adult target is about 0.5 mL/kg/h, which is 30–50 mL/h for 70 kg. Below it, add fluid by about 20–25% and recheck. Above it, reduce.
Hour 6. Same patient, still on the formula rate, now passing 90 mL/h of urine.
What is your next step?

choices.label: Lower the rate and recheck the urine next hour
Raise the rate 25% to keep pace with the output
Keep the calculated rate; nothing has changed
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask whether a patient passing 90 mL/h of urine is short of fluid.
That is not the right choice.
Rising output can look like demand, so more fluid seems logical. But good output means the tissues are full, and extra fluid risks pulmonary oedema and compartment syndromes.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so trace where extra fluid goes once the tissues are already full.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Nothing on the chart has changed, so the calculated rate feels right. But the urine has moved, and the rate is meant to follow it.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember the rate is reset by the urine each hour, not fixed at the start.

say.text: Trace it. Urine at 90 mL/h means the tissues are well filled, so the rate comes down.
Excess fluid is what causes pulmonary oedema and compartment syndromes, so check the urine again at the next hour.
Your patient arrives with a drip already running. The time of burn and the TBSA are confirmed.
Which step comes next?

choices.label: Start the full formula rate on top of the running drip
Stop the drip and restart the formula from zero
Subtract fluid already given from the first-8-hour volume
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what the patient has already received, and whether the formula should count it.
That is not the right choice.
It is tempting, because the formula is the number you learned, so it feels like the whole order. But the first-half target already allows for what has been given, so the drip counts toward it.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check what the first-half figure is meant to cover.

say.text: Count the 8 hours from the time of burn, not from arrival at hospital. The first-half target is the total for those hours.
Subtract what has already been given, then spread the rest over the hours left.
An 18 kg child has a 25% scald. What hourly urine target do you set?

choices.label: 10 mL/h, about 0.5 mL per kg per hour
18 mL/h, about 1 mL per kg per hour

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Tempting, because one adult number is the one you learned first. But a child's target is judged per kilogram, so an adult-based figure, halved or left whole, misses it.
A child's target is set per kilogram, about 1 mL/kg/h. That is higher than the adult 0.5 mL/kg/h, because a child's kidneys are smaller and the metabolic rate is higher.
A 70 kg adult has an electrical burn, and the urine shows pigment from muscle breakdown.
What hourly urine target do you set?

choices.label: 20 mL/h, the same figure used for a child
About 75–100 mL/h, a higher target to flush pigment

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Tempting, because a familiar number feels safe. But the injury sets the target: pigment threatens the tubules, so a routine target is too low here.
Electrical burns and rhabdomyolysis need more flow to keep the kidneys clear: about 1–1.5 mL/kg/h, so about 75–100 mL/h in a 70 kg adult.
Alkalinising the urine is not routinely needed if the output is adequate.
A 2-year-old was sized with the adult chart and came out at 40%.
Before you set the first-8-hour volume, what changes?

choices.label: Re-size with a Lund and Browder chart, then calculate
Keep 40%; the adult chart is close enough in a child
Keep 40%, but reduce only the legs for a child

say.text: That is not the right choice.

Tempting, because the adult chart is quick and the child's error looks small. But in a child the head is a bigger share and the legs a smaller one, so every adult figure misstates the size and the volume built on it.
The Lund and Browder chart corrects for age. The adult rule of nines overestimates a child's legs and underestimates the head.
Count only partial-thickness and full-thickness areas, then calculate the volume from the corrected size.
Which of these burns needs an escharotomy?

choices.label: Circumferential deep partial-thickness forearm burn with blisters
Circumferential full-thickness forearm burn with falling distal pulses
Superficial burn over the whole chest with normal ventilation

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Each of these keeps a feature that sounds serious and drops the qualifier that makes the eschar dangerous: a full-thickness burn, or a constricting ring with falling pulses or restricted ventilation.
Escharotomy is for circumferential full-thickness burns of a limb or chest, where inelastic eschar constricts as the swelling builds.
Incisions go through eschar only, along the midlateral and midaxial lines, and can be made at the bedside without anaesthesia because full-thickness skin is insensate.
